text: Tech sector crash minus 78%. That is what one scenario did to a portfolio of three invented chip stocks, $10,000 taken down to 2200. Where does 78 come from? Let me take it apart. Hi, this is Tanmay Kulkarni in for Humanitarian's AI. This week I contributed to mycroft, a book in a working repository of finance pipelines and it calls them recipes. One of them, the scenario stress testing agent shocks a portfolio with a name scenario and reports what is left. The portfolios here are mine invented. The tickers come from the workflows own list. The numbers are scenario arithmetic, not predictions and not investment advice. A scenario is a short list of named

Shocks. Tech sector crash names five. Four are price shocks, market minus 15%, technology sector minus 30, semiconductors minus 35 and AI stocks minus 40. The fifth is a volatility number. The engine's rule is simple. For each holding, add up the shocks that belong to it. Hold a guess. If the market alone falls 15%, how far does the biggest holding fall? Take the biggest holding, a chip designer. Everything belongs to the market, so a block of minus 15. It is a semiconductor stock, so minus 35. And it is on the AI list, so minus 40. The engine adds them, minus 90. The workflows own read me prints this exact

Sum as its worked example, which is a big part of why it is so easy to check. It even names a different way to combine them, so the rule is a choice you can see. The third holding is a chip maker that is not on the AI list. A block of minus 15 for the market, minus 35 for semiconductors. That is minus 50, not 90. The second chip stock takes minus 90 like the first. Now give each its share, 40% 30 30. 36 plus 27 plus 15 makes 78 and there is the number. A smaller scenario shows the same rule. An aggressive rate hike, market minus

10%, growth stocks minus 20, technology sector minus 15. Four growth names equal shares. Three of them take minus 30. One is also filed under the technology sector, so a third block lands on it and it takes minus 45. The book loses 33.75%, which the workflow labels critical. It's word for losses above 30. Here is the part I wanted to be sure of. To check the original, I wrote a second adder, a Python copy of the engine in its first steps, and ran both on the same portfolios. The original code comes straight out of the workflow file. On 24 requests, every number, every label, and every message matched. Then, I added 12

Deliberate breaks to my checks, and each one was caught. Before any adding, a validator reads each portfolio with the workflow's own rules and one addition of mine, and it protects the sum. Portfolios whose shares total 6/10 or 1.2 are accepted because the workflow rescales them to one. A holding with no ticker, a share that is not a number, an empty list, each is stopped with its reason written down. 10 out of 10 of my deliberately flawed portfolios, a sum of nothing never reaches the screen. Nothing here calls the outside world. The call to a model, the market data request, and the reply to a caller are

Written down as handoffs, not approved. Five items in the recipe are still open, and it says draft on purpose. That leaves a good list for next time. So, next time a stress test gives you one number, ask what was added, which shocks from which lists, and has anyone run the adder beside the original. A good answer names the terms. This was Tanmay Kulkarni for Humanitarian's AI. The contribution is pull request 74 on the Mycroft repository.
